items.prompt: A company needs to discover sensitive data in Amazon S3 and identify buckets with risky access settings. Which AWS service is designed for this requirement?
constraints: The data is stored in Amazon S3.
The company needs managed sensitive-data discovery and classification.
The requirement is data exposure visibility, not runtime workload threat detection.

options.text: Use Amazon Macie to discover and classify sensitive data in S3 and report relevant S3 security findings.
Use Amazon Inspector because it classifies the contents of S3 objects for sensitive information.
Use Amazon Detective because its behavior graph scans every S3 object for personal data.
Use AWS WAF because web ACLs identify sensitive records stored in S3 objects.

feedback.Reason: Amazon Macie is the AWS service for discovering and classifying sensitive data in Amazon S3 and helping assess S3 data security.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie analyzes S3 object data and bucket-level security posture using managed or custom data identifiers and produces findings for relevant issues.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team enables Macie for the required account and Region, selects S3 coverage, and reviews sensitive-data discovery and policy findings.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector focuses on software vulnerabilities, Detective supports investigations, and WAF filters web requests rather than classifying S3 object content.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Macie is specialized for S3 data discovery; it does not replace runtime threat detection, vulnerability scanning, or web request filtering.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector scans supported compute and package targets for vulnerabilities; it does not classify S3 object contents as Macie does.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Detective provides investigation context and behavior graphs, not object-content classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: WAF evaluates web requests associated with protected resources and does not inspect S3 data for sensitive identifiers.

items.prompt: An architect is asked to use Macie to inspect sensitive data in an Amazon DynamoDB table and an EBS volume. What is the correct response?
constraints: The requirement names two non-S3 data stores.
The team wants a managed AWS classification service.
The design must match the service's supported data scope.

options.text: Explain that Macie is focused on sensitive-data discovery in Amazon S3 and choose separate controls for the other data stores.
Enable Macie and assume it automatically mounts EBS volumes and reads DynamoDB attributes.
Use GuardDuty because it classifies every database field and EBS block for sensitive data.
Attach a WAF web ACL to the table and volume so Macie can inspect them indirectly.

feedback.Reason: Macie’s sensitive-data discovery scope is Amazon S3, so the architecture must not imply automatic inspection of unrelated stores.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie analyzes S3 buckets and objects in the supported service model. Data classification for DynamoDB or EBS requires controls appropriate to those services and their access paths.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect keeps Macie for S3 and evaluates service-specific classification, logging, or application controls for DynamoDB and EBS.
Details.errorCorrection: Macie does not transparently mount EBS or inspect every DynamoDB attribute, GuardDuty is not a data classifier, and WAF cannot be attached to those stores for this purpose.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A service-specific design may use more than one control, but it preserves accurate coverage claims and avoids false assurance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie’s supported discovery model is centered on S3, not transparent inspection of EBS blocks and DynamoDB attributes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GuardDuty detects threats and suspicious activity; it does not classify all database and volume content.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: WAF protects supported web-facing request paths and is not a data-classification mechanism for DynamoDB or EBS.

items.prompt: A security team needs continuing visibility into sensitive data appearing in a changing S3 estate, without manually selecting every object for each review. Which Macie capability is the best fit?
constraints: The S3 estate changes over time.
The team needs ongoing discovery coverage.
The team accepts service-defined sampling and coverage behavior.

options.text: Use Macie automated sensitive data discovery for ongoing analysis, then use targeted jobs when deeper coverage is required.
Run a one-time Inspector scan of the S3 bucket because Inspector automatically classifies new objects forever.
Create a CloudFront distribution because edge caching continuously scans object contents for identifiers.
Use a single GuardDuty finding because one detection proves that future S3 objects contain no sensitive data.

feedback.Reason: Macie automated sensitive data discovery is intended to provide ongoing visibility for S3 data while targeted discovery jobs can address specific coverage needs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Automated discovery uses Macie’s supported discovery process to sample and classify S3 data over time. A discovery job provides more explicit scope and scheduling control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team enables automated discovery for broad visibility and creates targeted jobs for high-value buckets or audit evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector is not the S3 sensitive-data classifier, CloudFront does not inspect object content for this purpose, and one GuardDuty finding cannot establish data classification coverage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automated discovery improves changing-estate visibility but is not a promise that every object is fully examined; coverage and job design remain explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service and a one-time scan does not provide Macie-style S3 sensitive-data discovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront delivers cached content and does not perform Macie sensitive-data classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: GuardDuty threat findings do not establish that future S3 objects are free of sensitive data.

items.prompt: A compliance team must recheck a curated set of S3 buckets every week and receive findings when new sensitive data appears. Which discovery-job configuration addresses the requirement?
constraints: The same S3 scope must be checked repeatedly.
The cadence is weekly.
The team needs findings from each run.

options.text: Create a scheduled Macie discovery job with the selected S3 scope and a weekly schedule.
Create a one-time Macie job and assume it automatically repeats when the bucket changes.
Enable an IAM access key rotation schedule because credential rotation scans object contents.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because expiration rules classify newly uploaded objects.

feedback.Reason: A scheduled Macie discovery job is the direct way to repeat sensitive-data discovery over a defined S3 scope.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie discovery jobs can be configured with an explicit S3 scope and schedule. A one-time job runs once and does not itself create a recurring control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team configures the bucket selection, frequency, identifiers, and finding behavior, then reviews job results and coverage after each run.
Details.errorCorrection: A one-time job does not become recurring automatically, IAM key rotation is unrelated, and S3 lifecycle rules manage objects rather than classify their content.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Recurring discovery increases coverage and cost; the schedule should reflect data sensitivity and operational capacity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A one-time job and a scheduled job have different execution behavior; a one-time job does not automatically repeat.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM credential rotation does not inspect S3 object contents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 lifecycle rules transition or expire objects and do not classify sensitive data.

items.prompt: A company must scan only production S3 buckets owned by the finance account and exclude a legal-hold prefix containing records that cannot be processed by the job. How should the architect reduce scope?
constraints: The job must not inspect unrelated accounts or buckets.
The legal-hold prefix must be excluded.
The scope must remain reviewable by the security team.

options.text: Configure the Macie discovery job with explicit bucket and object-selection criteria, including the required exclusions, and document the resulting scope.
Run the job against every bucket and delete findings for the legal-hold prefix afterward.
Use an SCP to hide the prefix from Macie because SCPs select individual S3 objects for discovery jobs.
Rely on the S3 bucket name alone because Macie cannot use object-level scope or exclusions.

feedback.Reason: Macie discovery jobs should be configured with deliberate S3 scope and exclusions when the requirement limits which objects may be examined.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A job’s S3 selection criteria determine the buckets and objects included in discovery. Explicit scope makes coverage and exclusions auditable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects only the production finance buckets, excludes the legal-hold prefix using supported criteria, and validates the job preview and results.
Details.errorCorrection: Scanning everything and deleting findings is not an access or processing boundary, SCPs do not select object prefixes for Macie jobs, and bucket names alone may be too broad.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Narrow scope can reduce cost and processing risk but may create blind spots that must be recorded and reviewed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Post-processing deletion does not prevent inspection and weakens evidence and scope control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: SCPs set account permission ceilings; they are not Macie object-selection filters.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A job can use supported object-selection criteria beyond a bucket-level boundary.

items.prompt: A discovery job must detect common credit-card numbers and AWS access keys in S3 objects. Which identifier strategy is the best starting point?
constraints: The team wants AWS-maintained patterns where available.
The job should detect both financial and credential data.
The team will review findings for context.

options.text: Select the relevant managed data identifiers for financial and credential patterns, then add custom identifiers only for organization-specific formats.
Use a WAF managed rule group because WAF identifiers automatically classify stored S3 object content.
Use only a bucket policy because policy statements recognize credit-card and access-key strings.
Disable identifiers and treat every object as sensitive because Macie cannot use detection patterns.

feedback.Reason: Macie managed data identifiers provide AWS-maintained detection patterns for common sensitive-data types, while custom identifiers address organization-specific formats.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie applies selected data identifiers during supported S3 discovery. Identifier choice affects what can be detected and how findings are interpreted.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects appropriate managed identifiers, tests representative data, and adds a narrowly scoped custom identifier only where the managed set does not meet the requirement.
Details.errorCorrection: WAF, bucket policies, and disabling identifiers do not perform Macie object-content pattern detection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed identifiers reduce authoring effort, while custom patterns require testing to limit false positives and missed matches.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: WAF rules inspect web requests and do not classify stored S3 object contents.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 bucket policies authorize requests and do not parse object content for sensitive-data patterns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Macie discovery relies on data identifiers and does not turn every object into a meaningful classification finding by default.

items.prompt: A discovery job must detect national identifiers in most countries but exclude a managed identifier that is not relevant to the company's operating regions. What should the team do?
constraints: Macie provides managed data identifiers.
The job should reduce irrelevant findings.
The team must preserve an explainable identifier configuration.

options.text: Review and select the applicable managed identifiers for the job, exclude irrelevant ones, and record the coverage decision.
Select every managed identifier permanently because more identifiers always improve precision.
Replace all managed identifiers with an IAM policy because authorization controls determine data patterns.
Turn off Macie findings so irrelevant identifiers cannot create alerts.

feedback.Reason: Identifier selection should reflect the data and geographic scope being assessed; irrelevant patterns can increase noise without improving the required coverage.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie discovery jobs use the configured set of managed and custom data identifiers. The configuration is part of the job’s detection behavior and should be reviewable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team maps required identifiers to data owners, excludes non-applicable managed identifiers, and tests the resulting findings against representative objects.
Details.errorCorrection: Selecting everything is not a precision strategy, IAM policies do not classify content, and disabling findings hides the signal instead of fixing the scope.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Narrow identifier selection reduces noise but must be revisited when data formats, countries, or compliance requirements change.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More patterns can create irrelevant findings and do not automatically improve precision for the stated estate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM authorization and sensitive-data pattern detection solve different problems.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling findings removes visibility instead of defining the correct detection scope.

items.prompt: An organization stores internal project codes in a format that no managed Macie identifier recognizes. What is the appropriate design?
constraints: The format has a documented pattern.
The organization needs Macie to report matches in S3 data.
The pattern must be tested to avoid broad false positives.

options.text: Create and test a Macie custom data identifier for the internal format, then include it in the relevant discovery configuration.
Create an IAM customer managed policy named after the code because IAM policies are custom data identifiers.
Use a security group rule containing the project-code regular expression so Macie can reuse it.
Encrypt the objects with SSE-S3 and assume encryption creates a searchable custom identifier.

feedback.Reason: Macie custom data identifiers let an organization define detection criteria for sensitive data types that are not covered by the managed set.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A custom data identifier uses organization-defined detection criteria and can be selected for Macie discovery. Testing is needed to balance matches and false positives.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team defines the project-code pattern, validates it against positive and negative samples, and includes it only in jobs that inspect the applicable data.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM policies authorize actions, security groups filter network traffic, and encryption protects data but does not define a Macie content pattern.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Custom identifiers increase coverage for proprietary formats but create an ownership and maintenance responsibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM customer managed policies are authorization documents and are not Macie data identifiers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security group rules control network traffic and cannot be consumed as content-detection patterns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Encryption protects confidentiality but does not make a pattern searchable or define a Macie identifier.

items.prompt: Macie repeatedly reports a known public test value that is intentionally stored in sample S3 objects. The value is not sensitive in this context. What should the team consider?
constraints: The value is stable and approved as non-sensitive.
The team wants to reduce repeated false positives.
The allow-list must not hide unrelated sensitive data.

options.text: Create a narrowly scoped Macie allow list for the approved value or pattern, review its ownership, and verify that it does not suppress real sensitive matches.
Disable all Macie findings because allow lists cannot be scoped to known values.
Delete the test objects after every scan so the finding history disappears.
Add the value to an SCP because SCPs suppress content matches across all accounts.

feedback.Reason: Macie allow lists can reduce known false positives when they are narrowly defined, approved, and reviewed for unintended suppression.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An allow list identifies text or patterns that Macie should exclude from sensitive-data discovery findings. It changes detection behavior and therefore needs governance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner records the test value, limits the allow-list pattern, tests nearby real values, and reviews the list as the sample data changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling all findings destroys visibility, deleting objects is not a control, and SCPs govern permissions rather than Macie content matches.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Allow lists lower noise but can create blind spots if a pattern is too broad or remains approved after the business context changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie findings should remain enabled; the issue is a known pattern, not a reason to remove all detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting test objects changes the sample rather than controlling detection and can destroy useful evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SCPs restrict account permissions and do not suppress Macie data-identifier matches.

items.prompt: A security dashboard must distinguish a sensitive-data discovery result from a bucket-access configuration issue. Which Macie concept should the architect use?
constraints: The dashboard must preserve finding meaning.
The two signals have different remediation owners.
The team needs to route findings to the right workflow.

options.text: Use Macie finding types and associated details to distinguish sensitive-data findings from policy findings, then route them by ownership.
Treat every Macie finding as a GuardDuty threat finding because all security findings have the same semantics.
Convert every finding to a WAF rule so the S3 bucket can block the reported content.
Discard the finding type and route only by the S3 bucket name because finding categories are not actionable.

feedback.Reason: Macie findings carry different meanings, including sensitive-data discovery and S3 policy findings, so routing should preserve the finding type.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie findings describe the nature of the issue and include resource and detection details. The finding category helps determine whether data owners or security administrators should respond.
Details.scenarioApplication: The dashboard maps sensitive-data findings to data owners and policy findings to the S3 security team while retaining the original Macie details.
Details.errorCorrection: Macie findings are not GuardDuty threat findings, WAF rules do not remediate stored object content, and bucket-only routing loses important context.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Type-aware routing improves response quality but requires stable ownership mappings and review when findings evolve.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GuardDuty and Macie findings represent different detection domains and should not be conflated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: WAF controls web requests and is not a remediation mechanism for arbitrary S3 object findings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The bucket alone does not explain whether the issue is data content or bucket policy posture.

items.prompt: Macie reports a high-severity finding for an S3 object containing customer identity data. What is the most appropriate first operational response?
constraints: The finding is a signal requiring verification.
The object may be accessible more broadly than intended.
The team must preserve evidence and reduce exposure safely.

options.text: Validate the finding and object exposure, preserve relevant evidence, and apply scoped S3 access remediation with the data owner.
Delete the entire S3 bucket immediately because severity alone proves every object is compromised.
Ignore the finding because Macie severity is only a billing classification and has no triage value.
Rotate every IAM credential in the organization before checking the affected object or policy.

feedback.Reason: A high-severity Macie finding should trigger evidence-led validation and scoped remediation of the affected S3 data and access posture.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie finding severity helps prioritize response, while the finding details identify the resource and detection context. The responder still validates exposure and chooses an appropriate control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team confirms the object and access path, restricts unintended access, records remediation, and checks whether similar data exists elsewhere.
Details.errorCorrection: Bucket deletion is destructive and disproportionate, ignoring severity loses a useful triage signal, and organization-wide rotation may create outage without addressing the object.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fast access remediation reduces exposure but must account for legitimate consumers, retention, and evidence preservation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A finding does not justify destructive bucket deletion without investigation and an approved recovery plan.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Severity is intended to support prioritization and should not be dismissed as billing metadata.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Broad credential rotation may not address the S3 exposure and can cause unrelated service disruption.

items.prompt: A central security team already triages findings in Security Hub and wants Macie findings included without building a custom polling system. Which design is appropriate?
constraints: The organization uses Security Hub as its central findings view.
Macie is enabled in the required accounts and Regions.
Finding ownership and workflow status must remain visible.

options.text: Enable the supported Macie integration with Security Hub in the relevant accounts and Regions, then verify finding synchronization and ownership.
Use CloudFront logs as the only bridge because Security Hub cannot receive findings from Macie.
Copy every Macie finding into a public S3 bucket because Security Hub only accepts public data.
Replace Macie with Inspector because Security Hub can aggregate only vulnerability findings.

feedback.Reason: Macie supports integration with Security Hub so the organization can centralize supported security findings and workflow.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The integration sends Macie findings to Security Hub according to account, Region, and service configuration. Security Hub then provides a central finding view and workflow model.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security administrator enables the integration, confirms the delegated-administrator scope, and tests that a Macie finding appears with useful source context.
Details.errorCorrection: CloudFront logs are not the Macie-to-Security-Hub integration, public S3 is unnecessary and unsafe, and Security Hub handles more than vulnerability findings.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralization improves triage but requires explicit regional enablement, account coverage, and ownership of status changes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CloudFront access logs do not provide the supported Macie finding integration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security findings should not be exposed through public storage, and Security Hub does not require public data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security Hub can aggregate findings from multiple security services, including supported Macie findings.

items.prompt: An architect must identify suspicious API activity against an S3 bucket and also discover whether objects contain regulated data. Which service pairing matches the two requirements?
constraints: The first requirement is behavioral threat detection.
The second requirement is S3 sensitive-data discovery.
The design should use each service for its intended signal.

options.text: Use GuardDuty for suspicious activity detection and Amazon Macie for S3 sensitive-data discovery and classification.
Use Macie for both API threat detection and object classification because Macie replaces all security monitoring.
Use Inspector for both requirements because vulnerability scanners detect API behavior and regulated records.
Use Security Hub alone because its dashboard directly performs all underlying detections without source services.

feedback.Reason: GuardDuty and Macie address different signals: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity, while Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty analyzes supported threat signals and produces findings about suspicious behavior. Macie analyzes S3 data and posture for sensitive-data and policy findings.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect enables both services where required, correlates findings in Security Hub if useful, and assigns behavior response separately from data-governance remediation.
Details.errorCorrection: Macie is not a general API threat detector, Inspector is for vulnerabilities, and Security Hub aggregates findings rather than replacing source detections.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Using specialized services increases coverage and operational integration work; service ownership and finding correlation must be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie discovers sensitive data and S3 policy issues; it is not the replacement for GuardDuty behavioral threat detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Inspector assesses vulnerabilities and does not provide both API behavior detection and S3 content classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security Hub aggregates and manages findings but depends on source services for their detections.

items.prompt: A release process must find vulnerabilities in container images and also locate personal data in S3 objects. Which service selection is correct?
constraints: Container image vulnerability scanning is required.
S3 object-content discovery is required.
The team wants findings with distinct remediation owners.

options.text: Use Amazon Inspector for supported ECR image vulnerability scanning and Macie for S3 sensitive-data discovery.
Use Macie to scan ECR layers for CVEs because all AWS security services share the same scanner.
Use GuardDuty to classify PII in S3 and scan container package versions for every CVE.
Use Security Hub without enabling source services because aggregation automatically scans images and objects.

feedback.Reason: Inspector assesses vulnerabilities in supported compute and package targets, while Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inspector provides vulnerability findings for supported ECR image targets and other supported resources. Macie applies data identifiers to supported S3 discovery.
Details.scenarioApplication: The release team routes Inspector findings to image owners and Macie findings to data owners, with Security Hub as an optional central view.
Details.errorCorrection: Macie does not scan ECR for CVEs, GuardDuty is not a package vulnerability or PII classifier, and Security Hub does not perform source scanning by itself.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate services provide accurate signal ownership but require a common severity, ticketing, and evidence process.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie is not the ECR image vulnerability scanner; Inspector owns that supported use case.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GuardDuty threat detection is not a replacement for Inspector vulnerability assessment or Macie data discovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security Hub aggregates supported findings and does not scan images or objects without source services.

items.prompt: An investigator needs to understand which principals and resources interacted during a suspected incident, while a data owner needs to know whether affected S3 objects contain regulated information. Which pairing is appropriate?
constraints: The first requirement is investigation context over activity.
The second requirement is S3 sensitive-data classification.
The services may be used together.

options.text: Use Amazon Detective for investigation context and behavior graphs, and Macie for S3 sensitive-data discovery.
Use Macie to reconstruct the full incident behavior graph because data identifiers explain principal relationships.
Use Detective to inspect every S3 object for credit-card numbers because graphs include object content.
Use WAF logs alone because a web ACL replaces both data classification and investigation context.

feedback.Reason: Detective helps investigators analyze behavior and relationships, while Macie addresses sensitive-data discovery in S3.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Detective organizes supported security data into behavior graphs and investigation context. Macie analyzes S3 object data with sensitive-data identifiers.
Details.scenarioApplication: The investigator uses Detective to understand activity and uses Macie to determine the data sensitivity of affected S3 objects before selecting containment and notification actions.
Details.errorCorrection: Macie does not build the incident behavior graph, Detective does not classify object contents, and WAF logs alone cannot supply either capability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Correlating investigation and data findings improves response but requires consistent resource identifiers and controlled access to sensitive evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie findings describe sensitive data and S3 posture; they do not reconstruct principal and resource behavior relationships.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Detective behavior graphs are not an object-content classification engine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: WAF logs cover a web request path and do not replace data classification or broader investigation context.

items.prompt: A security account must manage Macie across Organization member accounts while application teams retain ownership of their S3 data. Which pattern is appropriate?
constraints: AWS Organizations is used for the account fleet.
The security account is approved for central security administration.
Member accounts must be explicitly enabled and monitored.

options.text: Configure Macie organization administration with the approved security account, enable member accounts and Regions explicitly, and preserve data-owner remediation responsibilities.
Use the management account root user for every Macie finding because Macie cannot support delegated administration.
Share Macie through Amazon VPC peering because security services are administered as network resources.
Enable Macie only in the security account and assume it automatically scans every member-account bucket.

feedback.Reason: Macie supports organization-oriented administration patterns, but account and Region coverage still must be enabled and verified explicitly.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An organization administrator can configure Macie for member accounts and manage coverage, while member-account data owners remain responsible for remediation decisions on their resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security account registers the supported administrator relationship, enables member accounts in required Regions, and routes findings to the owning teams.
Details.errorCorrection: Routine root-user use is unsafe, VPC peering is unrelated to service administration, and enabling only one account does not automatically establish complete member coverage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central administration improves consistency but creates lifecycle, Region, permission, and coverage-monitoring responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Organization administration is intended to avoid routine management-account root operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: VPC peering connects networks and is not the Macie account-administration model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Member-account and Regional Macie coverage must be configured and verified; one account does not imply complete fleet scanning.

items.prompt: A company wants Macie coverage for a large archive but has a strict monthly budget. Which architecture decision best balances coverage and cost?
constraints: The archive contains mixed-sensitivity data.
The budget is limited.
The company must state the resulting coverage honestly.

options.text: Prioritize high-value buckets, use automated discovery or targeted scheduled jobs deliberately, tune identifiers and scope, and document excluded data and residual risk.
Enable every identifier and scan every object at the highest frequency because cost does not affect architecture quality.
Disable Macie and claim that S3 encryption provides equivalent sensitive-data discovery coverage.
Scan one representative object and extrapolate that all archive objects have the same classification.

feedback.Reason: Macie coverage should be designed against data value, discovery mode, scope, identifier selection, and budget; excluded coverage must remain explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Automated discovery and discovery jobs have different control and coverage characteristics. S3 scope, object selection, and identifier choices influence processing and findings.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect starts with regulated and high-value buckets, schedules deeper jobs where necessary, monitors cost and coverage, and records what is not inspected.
Details.errorCorrection: Scanning everything without a budget model is not a design, encryption does not classify data, and one object cannot represent a heterogeneous archive.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cost-aware scope can leave residual risk; the business must accept that risk or fund broader discovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Maximum scope and frequency can be unnecessarily expensive and does not satisfy a strict budget constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Encryption protects data but does not provide sensitive-data discovery or classification.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A representative object cannot establish classification for a heterogeneous archive.

items.prompt: An S3 object is flagged by Macie for sensitive data and the same account has a GuardDuty finding for suspicious access. What is the best response architecture?
constraints: The findings represent different detection domains.
The team must investigate access and data exposure together.
Containment must be scoped and evidence must be preserved.

options.text: Correlate the Macie and GuardDuty findings in the central security workflow, investigate the access path, preserve evidence, and apply scoped data and credential containment.
Close the Macie finding because GuardDuty already proves the object is malicious and no separate data review is needed.
Delete the object and the entire account before determining whether the access was authorized or whether retention applies.
Use Inspector to resolve the incident because a vulnerability finding automatically explains the S3 access event.

feedback.Reason: Macie and GuardDuty findings provide complementary signals, so incident response should correlate them and preserve both data and activity context before scoped containment.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Macie identifies sensitive-data or S3 policy conditions, while GuardDuty identifies suspicious activity. Security Hub or an incident platform can centralize findings, but responders still investigate the source details.
Details.scenarioApplication: The responder confirms the principal and request path, restricts unintended access, rotates or disables compromised credentials when warranted, and records the data exposure decision.
Details.errorCorrection: One finding does not replace the other, account or object deletion may destroy evidence and violate retention, and Inspector does not explain S3 access behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-service correlation improves diagnosis but requires synchronized timestamps, permissions, and ownership across the security and data teams.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Macie and GuardDuty answer different questions; closing one finding discards relevant data-exposure context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Destructive deletion before investigation can destroy evidence and violate retention or recovery requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Inspector vulnerability findings do not automatically explain an S3 access event or sensitive-data finding.
